posts.post_title: Product of Heritability and Selection Differential
posts.post_content: The product of realized heritability & selection differential is known as:

meta_input._aimcq_explanation:
Correct Answer: Response to selection

The Response to selection (R) — also called genetic gain per generation — is defined by the Breeder's Equation as the product of narrow-sense (realized) heritability and the selection differential.

Breeder's Equation

R = h² × S

  • h² = Realized (narrow-sense) heritability = VA / VP
  • S = Selection differential = Mean of selected parents − Population mean
  • S = i × σP (where i = intensity of selection, σP = phenotypic standard deviation)
Extended Form

R = h² × S = i × h² × σP = i × σA × rAP

Why Other Options Are Wrong
  • Limit of selection: The plateau reached when genetic variance is exhausted or inbreeding depression offsets gains.
  • Intensity of selection (i): The standardised selection differential = S/σP.
  • Accuracy of selection (rAP): Correlation between true breeding value and the selection criterion used.

posts.post_content: Heritability in the narrow sense is:

_aimcq_options.text: Always less than or equal to broad sense heritability

posts.post_content: Reappearance of an ancestral trait, after several generations, is known as:

meta_input._aimcq_explanation:
Correct Answer: Atavism

Atavism is the reappearance of an ancestral character that has been absent for several generations. It occurs when previously suppressed or silent genes (recessive alleles or dormant gene combinations) are re-expressed.

Key Facts — Atavism
  • Mechanism: Re-activation of dormant recessive genes or specific gene combinations that were masked in intermediate generations.
  • Example in animals: Occasional polydactyly in horses (extra toes, resembling ancestral Eohippus); striping in some horse breeds.
  • Distinguished from mutation: Atavism is not a new change — it is revival of an old one.
Why Other Options Are Wrong
  • Epistasis: One non-allelic gene masks expression of another — a current gene interaction, not a generational reappearance.
  • Mutation: A sudden heritable change in genetic material — a new alteration, not revival of an old trait.
  • Heterosis: Increased performance of offspring over parents due to heterozygosity — unrelated to ancestral trait reappearance.

posts.post_content: In H.W. equilibrium, genotypic frequency of heterozygote will be highest when gene frequency of one gene is-

Correct Answer: 0.50

In Hardy-Weinberg equilibrium, the frequency of heterozygotes is 2pq. This expression reaches its maximum value when p = q = 0.5, giving 2pq = 2 × 0.5 × 0.5 = 0.50 (50%).

Mathematical Proof
  • Heterozygote frequency: H = 2pq; where p + q = 1, so q = 1 − p
  • H = 2p(1−p) = 2p − 2p²
  • To maximise: dH/dp = 2 − 4p = 0 → p = 0.5
  • Maximum H = 2 × 0.5 × 0.5 = 0.50
Key Notes on Heterozygote Frequency
  • Frequency of heterozygotes (2pq) cannot exceed 50%
  • Maximum is achieved when p = q = 0.5
  • H-W equation: p² + 2pq + q² = 1
  • p + q = 1 (sum of all allele frequencies = 1)
  • P + H + Q = 1 (sum of all genotypic frequencies = 1)

posts.post_title: Sudden Heritable Change in Genetic Material
posts.post_content: Sudden heritable change in genetic material is known as:

meta_input._aimcq_explanation:
Correct Answer: Mutation

A mutation is a sudden, random, and heritable change in the genetic material (DNA sequence or chromosome structure). The term was coined by Hugo de Vries, who proposed the Mutation Theory of Evolution based on his work with Oenothera lamarckiana (Evening primrose).

Types of Mutation
TypeSub-typesDetails

  • It is the slowest force to change gene frequency (rate: 10⁻⁵ to 10⁻⁶ per locus per generation).
  • Multiple alleles are produced by mutation.
Why Other Options Are Wrong
  • Recombination: Re-assortment of existing alleles during meiosis — not a new change in genetic material.
  • Segregation: Mendel's first law — separation of alleles into gametes; not a change in genetic material.
  • Migration: Movement of individuals (gene flow) between populations — shifts gene frequencies, does not alter the genetic material itself.

  • Trait expressed in only one sex

posts.post_title: Calculating Gene Frequencies from Genotypic Data
posts.post_content: If genotypic frequency of dominant homozygote is $P=0.05$ and genotypic frequency recessive homozygote is $Q=0.65$ then find out the gene frequencies p & q-

meta_input._aimcq_explanation:
Correct Answer: p = 0.20 & q = 0.80

Using Hardy-Weinberg formulas, gene frequencies (p and q) can be calculated from known genotypic frequencies using the relationships between allele frequencies and homozygote proportions.

Step-by-Step Calculation
  • Given: P (dominant homozygote AA) = 0.05; Q (recessive homozygote aa) = 0.65
  • Step 1 — Find H: P + H + Q = 1 → H = 1 − 0.05 − 0.65 = 0.30
  • Step 2 — Find p: p = P + ½H = 0.05 + ½(0.30) = 0.05 + 0.15 = 0.20
  • Step 3 — Find q: q = Q + ½H = 0.65 + 0.15 = 0.80 (or simply q = 1 − p = 0.80)
  • Verification: p + q = 0.20 + 0.80 = 1.00 ✔
Hardy-Weinberg Key Formulas
ParameterFormula
Gene frequency p from genotypesp = P + ½H
Gene frequency q from genotypesq = Q + ½H
Genotypic frequency PP = p²
Genotypic frequency HH = 2pq
Genotypic frequency QQ = q²
Why Other Options Are Wrong
  • p=0.80 & q=0.20 → values reversed; q must be larger because Q (recessive homozygote) = 0.65 is dominant
  • p=0.40 & q=0.60 → does not satisfy p = P + ½H = 0.05 + 0.15 = 0.20
  • p=0.30 & q=0.50 → p + q ≠ 1 (0.30 + 0.50 = 0.80); violates fundamental H-W rule

posts.post_title: Genes Located on the Same Chromosome
posts.post_content: Two genes of two different traits located on the same chromosome are said to be:

meta_input._aimcq_explanation:
Correct Answer: Linked

Genes located on the same chromosome are called linked genes. Because they are physically connected on the same DNA molecule, they tend to be inherited together, defying Mendel's Law of Independent Assortment. Linkage was discovered by T.H. Morgan.

Key Facts — Linkage
  • Linkage is the exception to Mendel's Second Law (Law of Independent Assortment).
  • The closer two genes are on a chromosome, the stronger the linkage (lower recombination frequency).
  • Crossing over in the pachytene stage of Prophase I can break linkage and cause recombination.
  • Linkage is a temporary/transient cause of genetic correlation (unlike pleiotropy, which is permanent).
Why Other Options Are Wrong
  • Alleles: Alternative forms of the same gene at the same locus on homologous chromosomes — not genes for different traits.
  • Independent: Genes on different chromosomes that assort independently — opposite of linked.
  • Epistatic: Refers to intergenic interaction where one gene masks another — not about chromosomal location.

Inbred lines are developed in poultry by sustained inbreeding (full-sib mating for generations) to produce highly homozygous, genetically uniform lines.
